profile.name: bunny hug
profile.tagline: An early 20th-century animal dance from San Francisco that sparked societal uproar.
profile.insight: In 1913, comedian John Bunny immortalized the controversial dance on film in 'Bunny Dips Into Society'.
profile.profile: The bunny hug was a popular dancing style performed by young people in the early 20th century. Believed to have originated in the Barbary Coast dance halls of San Francisco, California, it emerged alongside other animal dances like the turkey trot and the grizzly bear. The dance was performed to American ragtime music and famously provoked considerable uproar in polite society.
profile.profile_long:
The bunny hug emerged as a prominent dancing style performed by young people during the early 20th century. Historical accounts place its origins in the Barbary Coast dance halls of San Francisco, California, where it developed alongside contemporaries such as the Texas Tommy, the turkey trot, and the grizzly bear. Reaching a peak of popularity between 1901 and 1910, the dance became part of a broader cultural wave of animal-themed dances that captured the attention of the youth while deeply unsettling traditional norms.

As part of the animal dance phenomenon, the bunny hug caused a notable uproar in polite society, challenging Victorian-era standards of decorum and public comportment. Despite or perhaps because of this controversy, the dance permeated popular culture in diverse ways. In 1912, composer Harry Von Tilzer and lyricist William Jerome released a dedicated song titled 'The Bunny Hug' with the subtitle 'the Craze of the Day'. The cultural footprint of the dance extended to the silver screen in 1913, when the Vitagraph comedy short 'Bunny Dips Into Society' featured scenes of comedian John Bunny performing the bunny hug, a film also distributed under the alternate title 'Bunny and the Bunny Hug'. The legacy of the style even crossed into mixology, inspiring a cocktail named the bunny hug in direct reference to the dance.

Musically, the bunny hug relied upon the vibrant and syncopated sounds of America's great ragtime composers. While specific technical descriptions of the footwork, posture, and spatial patterns are not detailed in surviving primary sources, its association with the vibrant dance halls of San Francisco and the wider ragtime era cements its status as a significant marker of early twentieth-century social dance history. The dance remains linked in historical lineages to other vernacular styles of the Barbary Coast, representing a moment of cultural shift driven by young dancers and popular entertainment media.
